Dustfall Calculations
The dustfall data in Table 10 assumes a background dustfall of 45 tons per square mile. (See Page 73, line 19, of the EIS.) This conservative value is representative of moderately dirty cities (McGill, Handbook of Air Pollution). The dustfall parameter is inherently a crude estimate of soiling potential. The calculations in Exhibit 4 indicate how dust control and staggered scheduling can minimize the regional impact of this project.
Particle Size Considerations
Particle size distribution was analyzed in order to address the question of potential health effects of demolition activities to residents in the immediate vicinity of the demolition activity. The most significant health effects associated with TSP are related to those particles which are respirable, i.e. 10 microns or less. An analysis of compressed or merged particles and original particles is not feasible by any commonly employed analysis technique. However, if compression of small particles into larger particles did occur, it would tend to reduce adverse health effects.
Conversion of TSP to 24 Hour Averages
The TSP concentrations were calculated for upwind and downwind conditions and for wood and brick buildings. (See Table 11 of the EIS.) 24-hour averages were calculated based on the conservative assumption that the 16-hour background TSP levels were 100

g/m and the TSP generated by the project were as shown. 24-hour averages were estimated as the weighted sum of the 8-hour conditions and the 16-hour conditions. For example, the 24-hour average for TSP downwind of a wood structure is (8 hrs x 33,644 + 16 hrs x 100)

Effects of Intermittent Control
Although the opportunities for dust sampling were limited for this EIS, it was possible to sample two different demolition practices: no dust control and extensive control, i.e., continuous wetting. It is reasonable to assume intermittent wetting would achieve a 50 percent reduction in dust emissions. It should be noted, however, that the measures to minimize harm include continuous wetting.
Diffusion Modeling
Diffusion calculations, employing a tilted plume model, indicate that the zone of impact could extend to a down wind distances of approximately 1000 feet: (See Exhibits 5-9). However, the model does not, consider the effect of barriers in the diffusion path. Also, the diffusion parameters for horizontal and vertical distribution of the plume, available for use with these models are not suitable for describing diffusion near the ground or an irregular terrain. Hence, the results of these calculations can not be interpreted as representative of the ambient air quality down wind of the demolition site.
